headline: AI agent built private LLM client/server with MQTT and 1,000 lines of code
summary: The author sought a simple way to access their home PC's Ollama LLM from their phone, avoiding complex networking. An AI agent created a minimal, secure solution using MQTT, without opening any ports.
details: The author aimed to access their home PC's Ollama LLM from a phone without the usual complex setup involving Docker, reverse proxies, VPNs, and open ports. Traditional methods presented too many moving parts and potential security vulnerabilities.

An AI agent developed a streamlined solution comprising a browser page, a small service on the PC, and a rented Linux box running an MQTT broker. This design ensures neither the phone nor the PC accepts incoming internet connections, maintaining home network security.

MQTT, a robust publish/subscribe message bus, serves as a secure rendezvous point. The phone publishes questions, which the PC, subscribed to the topic, receives and processes with Ollama. Answers are then streamed back via MQTT, with only the broker aware of the home network's existence.

While alternatives like Tailscale offer zero open ports, they require client installations on every device. Cloudflare Tunnel exposes an HTTP service, necessitating custom authentication. Direct port forwarding, which exposes the GPU box to the internet, was a risk the author wanted to avoid.

The entire system is remarkably lightweight, eschewing containers, reverse proxies, dedicated authentication services, or databases. The rented infrastructure, which runs Mosquitto and Nginx, handles several other tasks, making this project an efficient use of existing resources.

The project was largely generated by an AI agent using AllSpeak, a language designed for AI collaboration, where code reads like English. Key components like the streaming mobile UI and GPU management logic were concise, facilitating quick human review.

Debugging revealed practical challenges, including MQTT silently dropping unframed test messages and OpenSSH refusing keys due to overly permissive home directory permissions (mode 777). These highlight the subtle issues that can arise even in minimal setups.

headline: US & UK navies launch 3,700-pound torpedo from robotic drone submarine in historic first
summary: The U.S. and British Royal Navies successfully launched a 3,700-pound Mk 48 torpedo from the uncrewed XV Excalibur drone submarine. This joint effort under AUKUS Pillar 2 validates weapon interchangeability and marks a significant step in autonomous warfare.
details: The U.S. Navy and British Royal Navy achieved a historic milestone by successfully launching a U.S. Mk 48 heavyweight torpedo from the Royal Navy’s uncrewed drone submarine, XV Excalibur. This proof-of-concept launch occurred on September 13 at the British Underwater Test & Evaluation Center in Scotland.

The 3,700-pound Mk 48 torpedo, typically deployed from manned submarines, was externally attached to the XV Excalibur using a specialized cradle. This demonstration validates the seamless mechanical, electrical, and software integration of an American kinetic payload onto a British autonomous platform.

Conducted under AUKUS Pillar 2, this project, designated Project Broadsword, aims to accelerate advanced defense technologies. The rapid execution saw the project go from approval by the Department of the Navy Rapid Capabilities Office to trials in just seven months.

The XV Excalibur is the Royal Navy’s Extra-Large Uncrewed Underwater Vessel (XLUUV), designed for autonomous or remote operation. It has previously served as a mobile underwater laboratory and was remotely controlled from Australia in 2025.

This successful launch is a key development in the fast-rising field of autonomous warfare, where systems operate with minimal human intervention. The U.S. Navy plans to continue aggressive follow-on acceleration with Project CUTLASS, focusing on advanced payload integration and tactical employment scenarios.
